sections.html:
Needs a tight-fitting lid as this species is known to jump.

Rasbora dusonensis is a cyprinid from Sumatra, Peninsular Malaysia and Borneo, found in larger river channels and peat swamp blackwaters. Its identity was unclear for decades before its redescription by Ng and Kottelat (2013). It is very similar to R. tornieri, which shares the Musi river with it, but has a bright yellow caudal fin with a broad dark margin, against carmine red in R. tornieri. One specimen measured 162 mm SL, although 95 to 105 mm is a more commonly reported adult size.

Known with certainty from Sumatra, Indonesia (from the Indragiri River, Riau province to the Musi River, South Sumatra province), Peninsular Malaysia (eastward and southward from the Bernam River system in Perak and Selangor states to the Endau River drainage in Johor state) and Borneo (from the Baram river basin in Sarawak state, Malaysia to the Barito drainage in South Kalimantan province, Indonesia).

The Barito river flows though the city of Banjarmasin which is given as type locality of the species by Bleeker with two rivers, the 'Banjer' or 'Duson' mentioned.

Has been collected from various habitat-types including larger river channels and more sluggish blackwaters associated with areas of ancient peat swamp forest which are typically full of fallen leaves, twigs and branches.

In the former the water tends to be murky with a more-or-less neutral pH whereas in the latter it's characteristically stained brown due to the release of tannins and other chemicals released by decomposing organic material, of negligible hardness and conductivity, and acidic (pH 3.0 - 6.0).

It also inhabits permanent bodies of water including pools, backwaters and reservoirs and is known to move into flooded areas during the wet season across some of its range.

In the Musi river, Sumatra, R. dusonensis occurs sympatrically with the similar-looking congener R. tornieri (see 'Notes').
Requires a relatively large aquarium with a minimum surface area of 120 × 30 cm or equivalent. Volume: about 108 litres.

Choice of décor is not as critical as water quality and the amount of open swimming-space provided.

We suggest keeping it in a large, well-planted aquarium or set-up designed to resemble a flowing river with a substrate of variably-sized rocks and gravel, some large water-worn boulders and moderate water movement.

The latter could be further furnished with some driftwood roots and branches plus some hardy aquatic plants.

In either situation a tightly-fitting cover is essential as this species may jump at times.

It's also intolerant to the accumulation of organic wastes and requires spotless water at all times in order to thrive meaning a stringent maintenance regime is essential.

According to stomach analyses of wild specimens this species feeds mainly on aquatic and terrestrial invertebrates, particularly insects.

In the aquarium it will accept dried foods of a suitable size but should not be fed these on an exclusive basis.

Daily meals of small live and frozen fare such as Daphnia, Artemia and suchlike will result in the best colouration and encourage the fish to come into breeding condition.

This species is peaceful making it an ideal resident of the well-chosen community aquarium, although as always when selecting compatible fishes proper research is essential and its adult size should be a consideration.

A community based around one of its native countries or river basins could make a worthwhile project with some interesting alternatives.

It's a schooling species by nature and ideally a group of at least 6 specimens should be purchased.

Maintaining it in decent numbers will not only make the fish less nervous but will result in a more effective, natural-looking display, while males will display some interesting behaviour as they compete with one other for female attention.
Mature females are noticeably rounder-bellied and often a little larger than males.

May not yet have been bred in aquaria although likely to exhibit an egg-scattering strategy with no parental care.

When the fish are in good condition they will spawn often and in a well-decorated, mature aquarium it's possible that small numbers of fry may start to appear without human intervention.

However if you want to increase the yield of fry a slightly more controlled approach is required for which several different methods have proven successful for congeners.

What is essential is to provide some sort of egg trap or barrier through which the eggs can pass in order to prevent the adults eating them.

Incubation in Rasbora eggs is temperature-dependant to an extent but usually takes between 18 and 48 hours with the young free-swimming 24 to 48 hours later.

Microscopic food such as Paramecium may be required initially, introducing Artemia nauplii, microworm, etc., once the fry are large enough to accept them.

The identity of this species was unclear for a number of decades prior to its redescription by Ng and Kottelat (2013).

The confusion originated with Brittan (1954) who misidentified specimens of R. tornieri as R. dusonensis and was exacerbated by Alfred (1963) who concluded that the holotype of R. dusonensis was conspecific with R. myersi. Kottelat (1991) subsequently considered R. myersi, a plain grey-coloured species, to be a synonym of R. dusonensis but this conclusion was incorrect and both species are currently considered valid (Ng and Kottelat, 2013).

R. dusonensis differs from R. tornieri in possessing a bright yellow (vs. carmine red in R. tornieri) caudal-fin with a broad, dark distal margin (vs. with or without a narrow dark margin), and a more slender caudal peduncle fitting 8.5–9.6 times in SL and measuring 10.4–11.7 % SL (vs. 7.9–8.8 times and 11.4–12.6 % SL, respectively).

Both R. dusonensis and R. tornieri are included in the R. argyrotaenia species group. Within this group the only other species possessing a bright yellow caudal-fin is R. aurotaenia, but R. dusonensis can be distinguished from it by possessing a subpeduncular stripe, sharply-contrasted midlateral and supralateral stripes with discrete edges, and a more slender body with depth fitting 4.0–4.8 times in SL (vs. 3.7–4.0).

Rasbora is among the more speciose genera in the family Cyprinidae with members distributed throughout much of Southeast Asia, and it has long been recognised as a 'catch-all' polyphyletic grouping. Liao et al. (2010) and Tang et al. (2010) proposed differing arrangements of the genus and related genera. Here on SF the system proposed by Liao et al. (2010) is retained for the time being since generic names such as Boraras and Trigonostigma are well-established in aquarium literature.

• Liao, T. Y., Kullander, S. O. and F. Fang (2010). Phylogenetic analysis of the genus Rasbora (Teleostei: Cyprinidae). Zoologica Scripta 39(2), 155-176
  • Tang, K. L., et al. (2010). Systematics of the subfamily Danioninae (Teleostei: Cypriniformes: Cyprinidae). Molecular Phylogenetics and Evolution 57(1), 189-214
  • Kottelat, M. (1991). Notes on the taxonomy of some Sundaic and Indochinese species of Rasbora, with description of four new species (Pisces: Cyprinidae). Ichthyological Exploration of Freshwaters 2(2), 177-191
  • Kottelat, M. (2012). Rasbora rheophila, a new species of fish from northern Borneo (Teleostei: Cyprinidae). Revue suisse de Zoologie 119(1), 77-87
  • Ng, H. H. and M. Kottelat (2013). The identity of the cyprinid fishes Rasbora dusonensis and R. tornieri (Teleostei: Cyprinidae). Zootaxa 3635(1), 62-70
